Greater mouse-eared bat (Myotis myotis) is a comparatively large vespertilionid, and its reproductive output reflects a slow life-history strategy typical of temperate-zone bats. Gestation proceeds over a period of 65 days [tg = 65 days] when females maintain a core body temperature typical of active flight metabolism, approximately 35 °C [T = 35 °C]. This extended gestational period is consistent with the energetic demands of developing a relatively large neonate, as newborn pups weigh approximately 5.9 grams [Wwb = approximately 5.9 grams] at parturition, a substantial birth mass compared to many congeneric species. A single offspring per annual reproductive event is the norm; females produce just one litter each year, resulting in a maximum reproductive rate equivalent to one pup per year [Ri = one pup per year]. This low reproductive output is offset by extended parental investment, as the lactation period and subsequent maternal care allow the juvenile to achieve a considerable body size before facing the challenges of its first winter.

As the suckling juvenile transitions toward nutritional independence, the weaning stage represents a critical developmental milestone. Under the same thermoregulatory conditions that characterise the active maternal period, the time since birth at weaning is approximately 42 days [tx = approximately 42 days] at 35 °C [T = 35 °C]. During this interval, the pup grows rapidly, relying entirely on milk before beginning to consume solid insect prey captured by the mother. The onset of weaning is marked by the pup's first exogenous feeding events, after which the juvenile gradually reduces its dependency on lactation. Field observations indicate that weaned young attain a body condition that supports their first foraging flights. The prolonged nursing period, relative to the gestation length, underscores the species' investment in producing an offspring that is well-prepared for independent survival. This developmental timeline is typical among temperate insectivorous bats, where a single, relatively advanced juvenile is produced annually to maximise overwinter survival prospects.

Following weaning, the juvenile enters a protracted sub-adult phase before attaining reproductive maturity. In Myotis myotis, puberty — as indicated by the onset of gametogenesis and the first activation of gonadal tissues — occurs at 502 days after birth [tp = 502 days after birth] under the thermal conditions typical of active metabolism (35 °C [T = 35 °C]). This remarkably long pre-reproductive period, spanning well over a year, represents a significant delay in the life cycle compared to smaller-bodied congeners. The extended interval likely reflects the time required to accumulate sufficient fat reserves and to develop the foraging proficiency necessary to support the energetic costs of gestation and lactation. Males and females both exhibit this delayed maturation, with first ovulation or testicular descent rarely observed before the second autumn of life. Consequently, most individuals do not participate in breeding until they are at least two calendar years old, a pattern that contributes to the species' characteristically low population turnover rate.

The adult body size attained by this species is among the largest within the genus Myotis. The ultimate wet weight of a fully grown individual reaches approximately 28.55 grams [Wwi = approximately 28.55 grams], a figure that notably exceeds the typical range of 4 to 10 grams reported for many congeners in field guides. This substantial adult mass is associated with a relatively low surface-area-to-volume ratio, which confers thermal advantages during torpor and hibernation. The growth trajectory from the neonatal mass of 5.9 grams [Wwb = 5.9 grams] to the adult asymptotic mass represents a nearly fivefold increase, achieved over the course of the first year of life. Fat deposition before hibernation is considerable, and adult body mass can fluctuate seasonally by several grams, peaking in late autumn. The species' large size is also reflected in its wing morphology, which is adapted for slow, manoeuvrable flight through cluttered forest understorey habitats.

Longevity data for Myotis myotis indicate a life span that is remarkable among small mammals of its body size. When measured under controlled conditions at a stable ambient temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C] — a temperature approximating the torpid state of hibernating individuals — the maximum recorded life span is 37.1 years [am = 37.1 years]. This extraordinary longevity, exceeding three and a half decades, is a defining feature of the species' life history and is consistent with the extreme lifespans documented in many vespertilionid bats. The extended survival is supported by a combination of hibernation, which drastically reduces metabolic expenditure, and a low annual reproductive output that limits the physiological costs of breeding.
